evidence.text: There's a lot of problems with the business model that I have. primarily - there are two. One is that it's 12% more expensive. The other problem is, I think that just offering this non-applicator tampons is a problem. Because people, women just don't use them as much. I would prefer you to be able to offer both, and whatever the company wants, it's up to them. I’m going to pass, okay.

turns.text: Hey there!

turns.text: Hi!

turns.text: Hi! Hello! Okay.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Who are you?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: My name is Claire. I have goodies for you guys.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Oh, we like goodies, Claire. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: For your nose bleeds. 100% organic cotton non-applicator tampons. And then of course...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Wait, what? Let me give this back to you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's for you Phil. Phil.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Nose bleeds. Nose bleeds.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What’s the name of your company?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yes! So my name is Claire Coder, and I’m the founder and CEO of Aunt Flow. And myself, I’ve experienced something that 86% of women have as well. And that’s getting my period unexpectedly in public. And there are three options to handle that situation. One, is just like 64% of women, they leave work or what they’re doing immediately. Of course, for businesses, this is lost work hours, and for women this is lost opportunities in a really awkward situation.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: They leave work?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: Okay, can I, I'm sorry to interrupt - is it really that unexpected? Or do you always have in your purse when you know it's around that time?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You do. You always carry around.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: You hope to. I've definitely been in a situation, I actually started this business because I was at an event called Start-Up Weekend. And I was locked into a building for 52 hours and I unexpectedly got my period.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: But with a purse.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: With a purse. But I didn’t have tampons with me because I didn’t think I was going to have my period. So some people carry tampons all the time. Not everyone.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I don’t.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yeah. Right.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Well, I mean you could carry it around and like support your menstruators in need, yes, but there are a lot of situations where that doesn't happen. And you're caught without a tampon, or you're in a bathroom and you don't have a coin to figure out how to use a coin-operated machine. And that's a huge problem as well.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's true.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So it's a really uncomfortable situation. And so it happens unexpectedly. And that's a huge, huge problem.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So you said three things happen. One is you leave work or wherever you are.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: You could leave work. So 64% of women have left work immediately to go to the store to get the products that they need.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: Oh okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How do you get data?

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: Where is the 64% coming from?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So we, uh, we partnered with Free the Tampons. Which Nancy....

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Free the tampons.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Free the tampons, yes. So in 2013, Nancy Kramer started this movement called Free the Tampons. She had a TED talk where she discussed how, if toilet paper is offered for free, tampons should be too. And so there’s this whole idea where there’s a lack of bathroom equality. And for businesses, especially startups in Silicon Valley, they really want to show that they support their women. And offering free tampons is a visible way to demonstrate they support female employees.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And so you would sell to those companies?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Precisely. So our business model is two parts. So we have a consumer facing side, and then we also sell to businesses. 70% of our company is selling directly to businesses. We sell these boxes, they offer them in their bathrooms, and they can refill them with our tampons. And we work primarily with their maintenance department to make sure they’re completely restocked.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And that box which looks like a big jewelry box, that just sits on the, in the restroom? Or...

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yep. So it sits in the restroom and it also can be wall-mounted as well.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Got it. And then you just come in and refill the box with tampons every so often?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Well, I don’t, but typically the maintenance company does.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Why would they buy the tampons from you instead of from Walmart or Costco?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Totally. So Aunt Flow is actually the only company that works directly with businesses to supply them with 100% organic cotton tampons. Now, the other options are Tampax, and typically with Tampax they either order through Amazon or Costco. So Amazon and Costco are our competitors, but for companies like Viacom, who we just met with yesterday, they are not going to order a box of 36 applicator tampons to put in their bathrooms for 53 floors.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What's the buying decision for a company like Viacom, whoever is doing the buying, to decide on they want to buy from you versus Costco or Walmart or Amazon.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And what have they been doing beforehand?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yeah, so there's a few different options. So Viacom for example have already been offering tampons. But, they just did a huge $130 million renovation on their building in Times Square, and it was all green initiative. So our products are non-applicator tampons. Which you can't really buy at Costco.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: Okay, I’m sorry, what’s a non-applicator tampon?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So if you look in your little baggie, those are non-applicator.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So, meaning there’s not an applicator piece to insert. It’s manually inserted.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And why is that important?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Because - they’re plastic applicators, usually.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: But how many women, must use an applicator just for whatever reason?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: A lot.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But aren’t there other non-applicator tampons out on the market?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Right. So I’m just wondering, can you buy them from Amazon?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I think it’s bulk.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So to clarify. There’s really one brand that does non-applicator tampons, and that is OB tampons. They’re really, really well-known in Europe. They sell, 86% of tampon sales in Europe are non-applicator tampons. While only 6% of purchases for tampons in the United States are non-applicator.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Why? Why is that?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I think one of the reasons is because it’s more difficult. That people who have been using tampons actually prefer to have an applicator.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So let's be clear. We started out with applicator tampons.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You did?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So in November of 2016 when we launched sales, we launched with our business-to-consumer side. And that was our buy-one-give-one subscription box for 100% organic cotton applicator tampons. And that's what you see here.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And how'd that do?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So this is still in the market. It's doing really well.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How much revenue are you generating?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: $5,000 a month. Right now we’re transitioning from applicator to non-applicator. So we completely stopped all marketing starting at January.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Because when we researched our current customers we realized that 75% of them actually wanted non-applicators. We started sending them to our customers and…

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Well, why not just offer both? Can you?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Well... We’re really, we really want to make sure that people have access to these non-applicators. They’re 53 percent less waste, they’re extremely less money to manufacture. And then for businesses, when we sell to businesses, it’s really for an emergency situation.They don’t want to stock with high quality applicator tampons, or people are going to steal a whole bunch.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: How much more expensive are you?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Comparable to, comparable to the other options. Like Kotex or Playtex.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Like more expensive comparable?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So we’re about 12% more expensive.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Got it.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Wait, I'm sorry. I'm having trouble understanding the value proposition for the customer. So if I'm JP Morgan, I'm this Chief Tampon Officer.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Would you stop that, Phil.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Whatever. You know. Chief Toilet Paper Officer. Whoever is doing the buying here. What is the value proposition? Is she focused more on price? Is she focused on the green aspect? On the convenience of the delivery? You tell us.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yeah. So. It's a little bit different for each company. For Viacom it was, they're already offering free tampons, but they wanted to produce 53% less waste. That's why they're going to non-applicator.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So for Viacom it was about going green.

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Right. And for Chase, it's to show that they support female employees. So recently in the news, Wall Street Journal just published how they're actually paying their women employees 15% less. And they really are looking for a way to visibly show that they support women.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But why through Aunt Flow as opposed to buying tampons at Amazon or Costco and giving them away. Why are they going through you?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yeah. A few different reasons. So of course for the green side, there's that. For the cost side, we're pretty comparable to the other options because our manufacturing is significantly less expensive, because we don't have the applicator. And then in addition, what was awesome about our consumer standpoint is we've created this national phenomena where we've been featured in over 50 local and national news pieces ranging from Forbes to Teen Vogue. I was on a TLC TV show talking about the company. And so Chase Bank recognizes, they want to align with a very progressive brand. And a brand...

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: What’s an article, what’s a sample article about? Like what do they say about you?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So one of the top headlines is 20-year-old drops out of college to talk about menstruation for a living and is changing the world one cycle at a time.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: You’re 20 years old?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: I try to not mention that, because I don’t want people to think that I’m not real or I’m actually running sh*t. But, yeah, I’m 20.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: You’re killing it. I’m trying to think what I was doing when I was 20. It wasn’t selling to JP Morgan. But I just wanted to pull back a little bit.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, I wanted to answer Phil's question a little more. Because I think there's something going on here.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What was it? oh yeah value prop.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I don't get it still for Chase. They can, I mean, they could buy OB non-applicator tampons in bulk. I'm sure OB produces them...

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: But people aren't following OB. OB is...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So it's important to Chase for them to align with you? That's the reason they're giving you the business? They want to align with you because you've been published, you've had some articles about you?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Young women.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It's like a...

A business that has national recognition for what we're doing. And in addition we also have a giving factor, or a giving piece, too. So for every 100 pieces that a business purchases, we donate ten. So that's our social enterprise component.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: But, but Claire, let's say I’m OB. And I'm going in right after...I’m going in right after you. I'm going to say to them, all of those reasons are total bullsh*t. The reality is, your employees are running home or having some problems at work, you're losing money because women are not as productive as they could be, and so I'm solving an

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: But it's not all about price, right, is what you're saying.

turns.speaker: James
turns.text: But I feel that’s bullsh*t, though. I think the main pitch - is that JP Morgan is actually going to save a billion dollars a year on productivity.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: No, I think it’s an employee perk or something. Where like…

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: There’s a variety, like I was saying, there’s a variety of reasons.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Well I get your thought.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What I’m saying is like we have Aesop soap in our bathroom. And there are 500 other brands that are lower cost. But we make some sort of balanced buying decision that’s like you know we’re willing to pay a little bit more for a better product to make our employees happy or more productive. And I feel like that would be the pitch, correct me if I’m wrong, that would be the pitch that you would go in with. We’re not the lowest cost, but we’re the best value.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So what happens when Aunt Flow 2 comes along. I’m just thinking about, thinking about barriers to entry here. And so how do you think about someone coming in and knocking you out of these big companies?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: Yeah. So I think about that in a few different ways. First, we’re pushing for the three to five-year contracts. So that’s one barrier. It’s our mission to really grab as much land as possible. And be able to really expand our brand so that people recognize us and know us. And that’s primarily why we’re raising money right now. Quite frankly, we don’t necessarily need the money if we want to grow at the rate that we’re growing. But. We know that it’s a situation where we need to get in front of as many people as possible so that they can start purchasing our products and more people know our brand.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So I think your barrier is actually share of wallet. So I think that I’m less interested in just the number of clients that you get. And I’m more interested in can you sell more product to JP Morgan or - any of these guys right? And I think if you could sell them soap and, you know, toilet paper and whatever else they might need, I think you then become a core supplier. And it then becomes harder for them to kinda knock you out

turns.text: Can I reel back. How much are you raising and what valuation?

turns.speaker: Claire
turns.text: So we’re raising $500,000 at a $5 million cap.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Here’s where I’m at. I think that you should really expand the product range as quickly as you can. turns.speaker: Claire

And there’s...

turns.speaker: Phil

turns.text: All right, that’s all right.
